paragraphs: Variational inference uses an adjustable probability distribution to approximate a model's uncertainty. More flexible distributions can improve that approximation, but they can also make optimization harder. This paper addresses that optimization difficulty by reducing the variability of reparameterization gradients, the estimates used to adjust the distribution during learning.

The proposed tool is a control variate built from a quadratic approximation of the model. A control variate provides a structured correction that reduces noise in an estimate. The authors set its parameters through a double-descent scheme. The method applies to reparameterizable distributions whose mean and covariance are known, including Gaussian distributions with different covariance structures.

Experiments show large improvements in gradient variance and optimization convergence for non-factorized variational distributions, which can represent dependencies between variables. The contribution therefore helps make richer approximations more practical to optimize. Its stated applicability depends on reparameterization and known distribution moments; the reported optimization gains are empirical findings for the inference settings studied.
neurips-2020-approximation-based-varianc.tldr: A quadratic control variate reduces gradient noise and improves optimization in experiments with flexible variational distributions.

paragraphs: Multi-agent imitation learning asks interacting agents to learn a task from expert demonstrations without receiving an environmental reward function. Learning becomes difficult when demonstrations must support many agents whose actions affect one another. This paper focuses on two linked challenges: using samples efficiently and keeping the learning approach scalable.

The proposed method, BM3IL, combines a Bayesian formulation of imitation learning with a multi-type mean field approximation. The Bayesian component is introduced to improve sample efficiency. The approximation addresses scalability by representing interactions through aggregate effects while distinguishing multiple agent types. Together, these components provide a framework for learning coordinated behavior from demonstrations.

The authors compare BM3IL with three leading multi-agent imitation learning algorithms across several tasks. These include traffic optimization on a real-world transportation network. They report significant improvements over every comparison method in all tested scenarios. These results support the combined approach in the evaluated settings, including a transportation application that goes beyond the synthesized tasks motivating much prior work.
neurips-2020-bayesian-multi-type-mean-fi.tldr: BM3IL combines Bayesian learning and multi-type mean field approximations to improve sample efficiency and scalability in multi-agent imitation.

paragraphs: An imitation learner must sometimes act in states that expert demonstrations never covered. Inferring the expert's reward function can help, but the inferred reward remains uncertain. A policy optimized for one representative reward can take excessive risks, while a policy optimized against an adversarial reward can become so cautious that its practical performance suffers.

BROIL handles this tension by combining Bayesian inference over reward functions with a user-specified risk tolerance. It optimizes a policy that balances expected return against conditional value at risk, a measure concerned with unfavorable outcomes. This makes uncertainty about the reward part of policy selection, while allowing the desired degree of caution to vary.

The experiments show that BROIL can move between behavior emphasizing return and behavior emphasizing risk reduction. The authors also report improvements over existing risk-sensitive and risk-neutral inverse reinforcement learning algorithms. The contribution is a way to choose among these behaviors through an explicit risk preference, with empirical support for the resulting policies in the studied settings.
neurips-2020-bayesian-robust-optimizatio.tldr: BROIL uses uncertainty over inferred rewards and a chosen risk tolerance to balance expected performance against unfavorable outcomes.

paragraphs: Randomized smoothing uses added noise to support guarantees about a classifier's resistance to adversarial changes. Much existing work relies on Gaussian noise and focuses on perturbations measured with the l2 norm. This paper develops a broader framework for certification that accommodates non-Gaussian noise and more general attack types.

The framework treats certification as a functional optimization problem. This perspective lets the authors analyze how the choice of smoothing distribution affects the balance between accuracy and robustness. They use that analysis to design families of non-Gaussian distributions suited to different perturbation measures, including l1, l2, and l-infinity attacks.

The proposed methods achieve better certification results than previous work in the reported comparisons. Their significance is both methodological and practical: noise selection becomes an explicit design decision tied to the attack setting, and the same framework can address several settings. The accuracy–robustness trade-off remains part of the design, so changing the smoothing distribution is a choice about which properties to prioritize.
neurips-2020-black-box-certification-wit.tldr: A functional optimization framework designs non-Gaussian smoothing distributions for stronger certification across several adversarial perturbation measures.

paragraphs: Identifying which input features matter is a different challenge from predicting accurately. Deep networks complicate this distinction because their nonlinear structure and unidentifiability make theoretical analysis difficult. This paper studies feature selection for analytic deep neural networks, seeking a foundation for interpreting which inputs are relevant to a learned relationship.

The authors analyze Adaptive Group Lasso with Group Lasso used as its base estimator. They prove selection consistency for a broad class of networks. This is a statistical guarantee about recovering the relevant feature subset as the available data grow. The covered architectures include deep feed-forward networks, convolutional networks, and a major subclass of residual networks.

The result gives feature selection its own theoretical support rather than relying on predictive success as evidence of correct interpretation. The work also provides further evidence that ordinary Group Lasso might be inefficient for neural-network feature selection and favors its adaptive version. The guarantee concerns the analytic network classes studied, while the criticism of ordinary Group Lasso remains qualified.
neurips-2020-consistent-feature-selectio.tldr: The paper proves feature-selection consistency for Adaptive Group Lasso across a broad class of analytic deep networks.

paragraphs: Multilingual pretrained language models can already place related sentences from different languages near one another in their representations. This paper finds that this alignment can improve when a sequence-to-sequence model trains on sentence pairs selected using its own encoder. The model's existing representations therefore provide material for another round of learning.

CRISS turns this observation into an iterative process. It mines cross-language sentence pairs, trains on those pairs, and then repeats the mining and training steps. The approach links two capabilities: finding corresponding sentences across languages and translating between languages. Better alignment supports the retrieval process, while training on retrieved pairs improves alignment and translation together.

The authors report state-of-the-art unsupervised translation results across nine language directions, with an average gain of 2.4 BLEU. Sentence retrieval on Tatoeba across sixteen languages improves by 21.5 percentage points in accuracy on average. After supervised translation fine-tuning, CRISS also exceeds mBART by an average of 1.8 BLEU, showing benefits in both unsupervised evaluation and supervised downstream use.
neurips-2020-cross-lingual-retrieval-for.tldr: CRISS repeatedly mines cross-language sentence pairs and trains on them, improving both sentence alignment and translation.

paragraphs: A robot learning to manipulate objects with two arms must coordinate continuous movements and adapt when objects move to different locations. This paper proposes an imitation learning framework built around the hypothesis that representing relationships in the environment can improve this generalization. The goal is to learn manipulation skills whose usefulness extends across object placements.

The architecture divides complex movement dynamics into elemental primitives. Each primitive uses a recurrent graph neural network to represent interactions over time. A high-level planner arranges these primitives into a sequence, while a low-level controller combines their movement dynamics with inverse kinematics control. This creates a hierarchical, modular system connecting task organization to physical movement.

On several simulated two-arm manipulation tasks, the method generalizes better and achieves higher success rates than the evaluated baselines. These findings support the proposed use of relational information within a hierarchy of movement skills. The evidence described concerns simulated manipulation, and the authors make the simulation code, data, and models available to support further use of the framework.
neurips-2020-deep-imitation-learning-for.tldr: A hierarchy of graph-based movement primitives improves simulated two-arm robot manipulation across different object locations.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets devices collaborate while keeping their training data decentralized. A common aggregation method averages model parameters, which requires participating models to share the same structure and size. This paper investigates a more flexible way to combine client learning when those architectural requirements would be restrictive.

The proposed method uses ensemble distillation. Client models produce outputs on unlabeled data, and those outputs train the central classifier. Knowledge is combined through predictions, allowing client models to differ in size, numerical precision, or structure. The authors state that the approach mitigates privacy risk and cost to the same extent as baseline federated learning algorithms.

Experiments span computer vision and language datasets, including CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, AG News, and SST2, with heterogeneous models and data. The authors report faster server-model training and fewer communication rounds than existing federated techniques in their comparisons. The findings make prediction-based fusion attractive when devices need different models and communication efficiency is an important part of collaborative training.
neurips-2020-ensemble-distillation-for-r.tldr: Ensemble distillation combines heterogeneous client models through their predictions and reduces communication rounds in federated-learning experiments.

paragraphs: Homomorphic encryption allows a server to run a neural network on encrypted inputs and return an encrypted answer. The client retains the private key, so processing can preserve input privacy without server-side decryption. The obstacle addressed here is computation: encrypted neural-network inference can incur substantial overhead even when multiple values are packed into each ciphertext.

The authors identify ciphertext rotations as a major bottleneck. In the setting described, a rotation costs roughly ten times as much as a ciphertext–plaintext multiplication. Falcon moves neural-network computation into the frequency domain and introduces a homomorphic discrete Fourier transform using block-circulant matrices. It also provides spectral convolution and fully connected operations combining those matrices with batched encryption.

These operations are designed to reduce inference latency while supporting computation on encrypted data. On MNIST and CIFAR-10, Falcon achieves reported state-of-the-art inference accuracy and reduces latency by 45.45% to 85.34% relative to prior encrypted neural networks. The results connect an identified expensive operation to a representation and computation strategy that improves measured inference speed.
neurips-2020-falcon-fast-spectral-infere.tldr: Falcon uses frequency-domain operations to accelerate encrypted neural-network inference while achieving strong accuracy on the evaluated datasets.

paragraphs: The squared Wasserstein distance compares probability distributions through an optimal transport problem. Estimating it commonly involves a discrete approximation, with entropic regularization making computation more manageable. This paper proposes using the Sinkhorn divergence, which adds debiasing terms, to improve the computational cost of estimating the same underlying quantity.

For smooth densities, the authors show comparable sample complexity while permitting stronger regularization. To achieve accuracy epsilon, the regularization can scale with the square root of epsilon rather than epsilon. This yields better computational complexity bounds and substantial practical speedups. The analysis covers both distributions represented by random samples and deterministic discretizations on uniform grids.

The paper also studies an estimator using Richardson extrapolation of the Sinkhorn divergence to improve statistical and computational efficiency further. Those additional guarantees require a regularity condition on the approximation error, which holds for Gaussian densities. Numerical experiments demonstrate the estimators' efficiency. The central result connects debiasing to greater freedom to regularize, with explicit smoothness and regularity conditions supporting the theoretical improvements.
neurips-2020-faster-wasserstein-distance.tldr: For smooth densities, debiased Sinkhorn estimators permit stronger regularization and faster squared Wasserstein distance estimation.

paragraphs: Credit assignment in reinforcement learning concerns how new information should change an agent's earlier predictions. Internal world models let an agent spend additional computation on this process through planning. This paper asks how that computation is best used, comparing planning that looks forward with planning that reasons backward from later states.

Forward models support forethought by predicting what can happen next. Backward models support hindsight by reasoning about what could have preceded a state. Through carefully constructed scenarios, the authors establish merits, limitations, and complementary properties of these mechanisms. Their comparison examines how the direction of planning affects the propagation of information within an agent's predictions.

The paper also studies which states should be selected for prediction updates, making the allocation of planning effort a central question. It then considers model estimation across a spectrum from predictors of environmental dynamics to models designed with the planner in mind. Together, these investigations treat effective planning as a combination of model direction, update location, and model purpose.
neurips-2020-forethought-and-hindsight-i.tldr: The paper examines how forward and backward planning complement one another in reinforcement-learning credit assignment.

paragraphs: High-resolution images can improve classification accuracy, but processing them can require substantial computation and memory. This paper starts from the observation that only some image regions are relevant to the classification task. Its framework builds a prediction from a sequence of relatively small inputs selected strategically from the original image.

Reinforcement learning guides which inputs the model processes. Because classification unfolds as a sequence, inference can stop once the model is sufficiently confident, avoiding additional computation. The framework can use many lightweight convolutional networks as feature extractors, including MobileNets, EfficientNets, and RegNets. This allows selective image processing to work alongside existing efficient network designs.

ImageNet experiments show consistent improvements in computational efficiency across a variety of models. In one concrete deployment measurement, the approach reduces MobileNet-V3's average latency on an iPhone XS Max by 20% without sacrificing accuracy. The result shows that adapting how much of an image is processed can provide additional savings even when the underlying network is already designed for efficiency.
neurips-2020-glance-and-focus-a-dynamic-.tldr: Strategic selection of small image inputs and confidence-based stopping reduce classification computation while preserving accuracy in the reported example.

paragraphs: A dynamic treatment regime specifies how to choose treatments over time using a patient's evolving characteristics and treatment history. Evaluating these rules from existing data is challenging because time-varying confounders influence treatment assignment. The resulting bias can undermine both estimates of a regime's value and the treatment rules learned from those estimates.

Gradient Regularized V-learning, or GRV, targets the value function used to assess a treatment regime. It regularizes the underlying outcome and propensity score models according to an optimality condition from semiparametric estimation theory. These components represent outcomes and treatment-assignment probabilities, connecting the method's statistical design directly to the confounding problem motivating the work.

Using this construction, the authors develop estimators described as efficient and stable with finite samples. Multiple simulation studies and one real-world medical dataset show superior regime evaluation and learning in their comparisons. The findings support the method as a way to improve the statistical basis for selecting treatments over time, with the reported evidence coming from these evaluations.
neurips-2020-gradient-regularized-v-lear.tldr: GRV regularizes outcome and treatment-assignment models to improve the evaluation and learning of sequential treatment rules.

paragraphs: A 3D human pose model can lose accuracy when it encounters scenarios containing poses unlike its training data. This paper proposes Inference Stage Optimization, or ISO, to adapt the model when source and target pose distributions differ. Its starting point is that unlabeled target inputs still contain useful information about the new scenario.

Before predicting a target instance, ISO updates the model through geometry-aware self-supervised learning on that instance. This makes adaptation part of inference itself. For sequential inputs, the authors also introduce an online version that streams the self-supervised learning process, allowing the framework to use a continuing sequence of target observations.

The authors analyze ISO across diverse benchmarks in cross-scenario settings and report that the online mode substantially improves its effectiveness. On MPI-INF-3DHP, the framework reaches 83.6% 3D PCK, with a reported improvement of 9.7% over the previous best result. These findings support adapting to unlabeled target data as a way to improve generalization across the evaluated pose distributions.
neurips-2020-inference-stage-optimizatio.tldr: ISO adapts a 3D pose model to unlabeled target inputs before prediction through geometry-aware self-supervised learning.

paragraphs: Few-shot learning requires classifying new examples from only a small labeled support set. In the transductive setting studied here, the unlabeled query examples also participate in inference. Transductive Information Maximization, or TIM, uses those query features alongside the support labels to adapt predictions for the particular task.

TIM maximizes mutual information between query features and their predicted labels while also applying a supervised loss on the support set. The authors introduce an alternating-direction solver that substantially accelerates convergence compared with gradient-based optimization while achieving similar accuracy. The inference procedure is modular and can operate on top of any base-training feature extractor.

Experiments use a fixed feature extractor trained on base classes with ordinary cross-entropy, without complex meta-learning schemes. Across datasets and networks, TIM delivers reported accuracy improvements between 2% and 5% over the strongest comparison method. Improvements also extend to tested scenarios with domain shifts and more classes, supporting task-specific transductive inference as a useful component of few-shot classification.
neurips-2020-information-maximization-fo.tldr: TIM combines support-label supervision with query-set information maximization to improve transductive few-shot classification.

paragraphs: Inverse reinforcement learning seeks the reward function behind observed behavior. Often, demonstrations show an expert acting near optimally, but some applications also expose how that behavior developed during learning. This paper uses a sequence of changing policies as evidence about the reward an agent is trying to optimize.

The proposed algorithm assumes the observed agent updates its policy parameters along the gradient direction. Under that assumption, changes between policies provide information about the objective guiding learning. The authors then extend the method to a setting where the available evidence consists of recorded learning trajectories rather than direct access to the sequence of policies.

For both settings, the paper provides theoretical insights into algorithm performance. It also evaluates the approach in a simulated GridWorld and in MuJoCo environments, comparing against a state-of-the-art baseline. The contribution is to incorporate the learning process into reward inference. Its central modeling assumption is specifically gradient-directed policy updates, which determines how observed changes are interpreted as evidence.
neurips-2020-inverse-reinforcement-learn.tldr: The method infers an agent's reward from its learning process by assuming policy updates follow a gradient direction.

paragraphs: Personalized federated learning allows collaborative training to account for differences among participating clients. This paper studies a particular optimization formulation previously used to explain local stochastic gradient methods. Its goal is to establish the resources required to solve that formulation and develop algorithms that meet those requirements.

The authors derive lower bounds for two resources: communication and local oracle work. Communication measures the exchange needed between participants, while local oracle complexity measures the local information-gathering operations used by optimization. These bounds establish targets against which algorithms can be judged. The paper then introduces several methods matching those targets in almost all regimes.

The methods include an accelerated FedProx variant and an accelerated, variance-reduced version of FedAvg or Local SGD. The authors identify these as the first provably optimal methods for the studied personalized federated-learning formulation. Extensive numerical experiments also show practical superiority. The optimality statement is tied to that formulation and the regimes where the lower bounds are matched.
neurips-2020-lower-bounds-and-optimal-al.tldr: The paper establishes resource lower bounds and develops personalized federated-learning algorithms that match them in almost all regimes.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a 3D surface from multiple images requires accounting for both object shape and how the object appears under lighting. This paper introduces an architecture that jointly learns the unknown geometry, camera parameters, and a neural renderer. The renderer approximates light reflected from the surface toward the camera.

The surface is represented as the zero level-set of a neural network: the locations where its output equals zero define the geometry. A separate rendering component is derived from the rendering equation and can implicitly represent a broad range of materials and lighting conditions. This gives geometry and appearance distinct roles within the jointly trained architecture.

The authors train on real object images from the DTU MVS dataset, covering different materials, lighting conditions, and noisy initial camera estimates. They report state-of-the-art surface reconstructions with high fidelity, resolution, and detail. These findings support the joint treatment of geometry, camera estimation, and appearance modeling for the varied image conditions included in the evaluation.
neurips-2020-multiview-neural-surface-re.tldr: A neural architecture jointly learns surface geometry, camera parameters, and appearance to reconstruct detailed 3D objects from multiple images.

paragraphs: Combining neural networks into an ensemble can improve classification accuracy and uncertainty estimation. This paper studies how ensemble quality changes with both the number of member networks and the size of each member. It examines negative log-likelihood before and after calibration, focusing on how the model assigns probabilities to labels.

The authors identify conditions under which calibrated negative log-likelihood follows a power law as ensemble size or member size changes. They also analyze how the parameters of these relationships behave. A practical finding is that several medium-sized networks can outperform one larger network with the same total number of parameters, an allocation they call a memory split.

The detected power-law-like patterns can help predict the benefit of adding ensemble members and the optimal memory split for a given budget. These predictions use a relatively small number of trained networks. The contribution therefore connects measured scaling behavior to model-allocation decisions, while preserving the conditional nature of the power laws and the possible advantage of an ensemble over a single network.
neurips-2020-on-power-laws-in-deep-ensem.tldr: Conditional power-law patterns help predict ensemble gains and how to divide a fixed parameter budget among networks.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks often receive a fixed graph chosen before training, but those connections may not best support the task. Learning an unrestricted graph is difficult because there are so many possible structures. Pointer Graph Networks address this problem by adding a sparse, adaptable set of inferred connections to sets or graphs.

Each node dynamically points to another node, and the network passes messages along these pointers. The sparse structure keeps learning tractable while remaining expressive enough to simulate complex algorithms. Crucially, the pointing mechanism receives direct supervision for long sequences of operations on classical data structures, introducing structural guidance from theoretical computer science.

The authors qualitatively demonstrate learned parallelizable variants of disjoint set unions and link/cut trees. On dynamic graph connectivity tasks, PGNs generalize to test inputs five times larger than those used in training and outperform unrestricted graph neural networks and Deep Sets. The findings show the value of supervised, adaptable pointers for the evaluated algorithmic tasks and larger-input generalization.
neurips-2020-pointer-graph-networks-3b50.tldr: Supervised dynamic pointers give graph networks a sparse learned structure that generalizes to larger inputs on connectivity tasks.

paragraphs: Quasi-Newton optimization uses approximations of curvature to guide parameter updates. Applying it directly to deep networks is difficult because millions of parameters make full curvature matrices, and even conventional stored update histories, impractical. This paper develops stochastic BFGS and limited-memory BFGS methods with structure tailored to neural-network layers.

The methods approximate the Hessian with a block-diagonal matrix, assigning a block to each layer. Each block is then represented as a Kronecker product of two much smaller matrices. This resembles the factorization strategy used by KFAC, though KFAC approximates the Fisher matrix. The authors also introduce damping to control both upper and lower bounds of their approximations.

That damping addresses the indefinite and highly variable curvature encountered in deep-network training. Tests use feed-forward autoencoders with nine or thirteen layers on three datasets. The proposed methods outperform or perform comparably to KFAC and leading first-order stochastic methods. These findings support structured curvature approximations as a practical training option in the evaluated autoencoder settings.
neurips-2020-practical-quasi-newton-meth.tldr: Layerwise Kronecker factorizations and controlled damping make quasi-Newton training practical and competitive in the tested deep autoencoders.

paragraphs: Autoregressive spike-train models are commonly fitted to predict the next time step by maximum likelihood. Yet good one-step prediction can coexist with poor behavior when the model repeatedly generates its own future inputs. Generated neural activity may miss important data features or even develop diverging firing rates.

This paper instead directly compares recorded spike trains with spike trains generated by the model. It uses spike-train kernels to define a maximum mean discrepancy, a measure of difference between the recorded and generated distributions. The authors develop a stochastic method for minimizing this discrepancy, making generated behavior itself the object of optimization.

Experiments on real and synthetic neural data show that the approach produces well-behaving models. Different combinations of kernels also let the authors control trade-offs among the spike-train features being matched. This matters when the model cannot reproduce every aspect of the data: the kernel combination provides a way to choose the balance among those features during fitting.
neurips-2020-rescuing-neural-spike-train.tldr: Directly matching generated and recorded spike trains improves recursive model behavior and allows control over which activity features are emphasized.

paragraphs: Graph pooling often groups nodes into clusters while preserving local relationships. This design borrows from convolutional image models, where nearby pixels form natural patches. The paper asks whether preserving locality during pooling actually explains the performance of graph neural networks on commonly used benchmarks, an assumption that had received little rigorous evaluation.

The authors modify representative graph networks with pooling variants that challenge this assumption. Some use randomization, while others cluster the complement graph, changing which relationships guide grouping. In the experiments, these variants produce no performance decrease. This makes locality preservation a directly tested architectural choice within the evaluated models.

To explain the result, the authors examine how convolutional layers interact with subsequent pooling layers. They find that convolution plays the leading role in the learned representations. Their conclusion is that local pooling does not account for the success of these networks on the relevant benchmarks studied. The work therefore shifts attention toward the representations formed before pooling when interpreting those benchmark results.
neurips-2020-rethinking-pooling-in-graph.tldr: Pooling variants that disrupt locality preserve performance in the studied graph networks, highlighting convolution's leading role.

paragraphs: Treatment-effect subgroup analysis seeks groups whose members respond similarly to an intervention, with meaningful differences between groups. Methods that focus on separating subgroup averages can overlook variation within each group. They may also depend on a particular individualized treatment-effect estimator and provide weak uncertainty estimates for the resulting analysis.

R2P addresses these issues through a subgrouping method that can use any externally supplied individualized treatment-effect estimator. It quantifies uncertainty in those estimates with a construction described as more robust than competing methods. This separates the choice of estimator from the partitioning procedure while bringing uncertainty into the analysis of treatment-effect groups.

Experiments on synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets based on real data produce groups that are more internally homogeneous and more distinct from one another than those from comparison methods. The authors also report much narrower confidence intervals with a prescribed coverage guarantee. Together, these findings support evaluating subgroup quality through within-group consistency, between-group differences, and uncertainty in the estimated effects.
neurips-2020-robust-recursive-partitioni.tldr: R2P combines flexible treatment-effect estimation with uncertainty quantification to identify more coherent and distinct treatment-response subgroups.

paragraphs: This paper introduces neural-network activation functions designed to reproduce properties associated with Matérn kernels in Gaussian processes. The family covers locally stationary models with different degrees of mean-square differentiability, providing a way to vary smoothness through the activation choice. The goal includes improving how Bayesian neural networks express uncertainty.

The authors establish an explicit connection to corresponding Gaussian-process models for a network with one infinitely wide hidden layer. At the infinite-smoothness limit, the Matérn family becomes the RBF kernel, and the proposed construction recovers RBF activations. This gives the activation family a defined theoretical relationship to established probabilistic models under that architectural limit.

Experiments show good predictive performance and uncertainty calibration when local stationarity is combined with limited mean-square differentiability. Local stationarity specifically helps calibrate uncertainty on out-of-distribution inputs. The evaluations include classification and regression benchmarks and a radar emitter classification task, supporting activation design as a useful tool for shaping uncertainty behavior in the Bayesian deep-learning settings tested.
neurips-2020-stationary-activations-for-.tldr: Matérn-inspired activations connect neural networks to Gaussian-process properties and improve uncertainty calibration in evaluated Bayesian learning tasks.
